sentences.text: Carinthiasuchus bore a series of bony plates, known as osteoderms, along its tail.
These tail osteoderms were shaped like drops, longer than they were wide, and displayed a central ridge with small tooth-like projections on uneven outer edges.
They were set in two parallel rows, with each vertebra supporting two or three pairs of plates.
Georg Kandutsch uncovered the holotype near Jadersdorf in the Gailtal Alps of Carinthia, Austria.
The holotype consists of portions of the skull, several caudal vertebrae, and an articulated distal tail.
The specific epithet kandutschi commemorates the discoverer Georg Kandutsch.
The type locality is recorded as the Partnach Formation.
All fossils attributed to this taxon were recovered in Austria.
Carinthiasuchus is presently regarded as a valid taxon.
The original description introduced both a new genus and a new species.
The preserved skull measures 53 mm, indicating a juvenile total length of up to 65 mm.
Unfused vertebrae and skull bones show that the specimen had not yet reached full maturity.
It is placed within the clade Poposauroidea.
Phylogenetic studies locate Carinthiasuchus among the early-diverging members of Poposauroidea inside Pseudosuchia.
Analyses suggest that assigning it to Poposauroidea fits the data better than linking it to other European crocodylomorphs or rauisuchians.
The animal lived during the Ladinian to Carnian stages of the Triassic period.
Its remains come from the Partnach Formation of Carinthia, Austria, spanning the Ladinian to Early Carnian ages.
